newsitem.title: USA: Way microbes change methane to methanol found.
newsitem.headline: Way microbes change methane to methanol found.

text.p: In a finding that could lead to huges changes in energy industries, researchers have found the tool that microbes use to convert methane, or natural gas, into liquid methanol, an article published on Thursday said.

Researchers at the University of Minnesota and Carnegie-Mellon University found a diamond-shaped configuration of iron and oxygen atoms in the enzyme that microbes use to convert methane to methyl alcohol, or methanol, the article in Science magazine said.

Chemists for years have sought ways to open up the methane molecule's structure enough to insert a single oxygen atom, and thus convert the gas that is difficult and expensive to contain and transport into a much more easily handled liquid.

"Methane is the smallest hydrocarbon, but it's the toughest nut to crack. It's the toughest to break down without completely burning it up," the University of Minnesota's Larry Que, the study's principal investigator, said in a statement.

By taking a "snapshot" of the enzyme in action with gamma rays and X-rays, the researchers found that when the bacterial enzyme was working, it formed a diamond-shaped structure every time it grabbed a molecule of methane.
Currently methane gas is converted synthetically into liquid methanol in a capital-intensive two-step process.
Understanding how the natural configuration works could help develop a cheap process to make methanol a less-polluting and cost-effective alternative to gasoline, the article said.
It could also help in developing new processes for making plastics and other chemicals now made from crude oil.
Conversion to liquid would also lower costs of using natural gas for cooking and heating homes, where a large part of the expense is from transporting the gas.

"It gives you an understanding of how the process can happen in nature and now we've got to see if we can duplicate it in the laboratory," said Raymond Lewis, director of the American Methanol Institute.
